topics.title: How Browsers Work
topics.informs: rendering strategy, layout/paint cost, animation performance, multi-process architecture
topics.takeaway: Browser = Messenger + Chef + Painter. It fetches, processes, and paints everything you see.

topics.title: Critical Rendering Path
topics.informs: LCP optimization, render-blocking CSS/JS, script loading (async/defer), font loading, preloading
topics.takeaway: CRP = The minimum steps browser MUST complete before showing ANYTHING on screen. Optimizing CRP = reducing what blocks those first steps.

topics.title: Browser Storage Mechanisms
topics.informs: client persistence, offline-first, auth token storage, caching, storage quotas
topics.takeaway: Each storage type exists for a different reason. Picking the wrong one causes security bugs, data loss, or poor performance.

topics.title: JavaScript Runtime & Event Loop
topics.informs: INP and long tasks, async data flow, Web Workers, scheduling UI updates, real-time update batching
topics.takeaway: JavaScript runs one thing at a time. "Async" does not mean "parallel JS" — it means "the browser does the waiting, and the event loop hands the result back to your single thread when it's free."

topics.title: DOM & Virtual DOM
topics.informs: DOM update strategy, framework choice (VDOM vs signals), list rendering performance, INP
topics.takeaway: the DOM is the browser's live object tree for the page. Touching it is not slow by itself — making the browser *recalculate layout and repaint* is. Virtual DOM, signals and compilers are just different strategies for running the *fewest* DOM operations with the *least* bookkeeping.

topics.title: HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3
topics.informs: asset bundling strategy, CDN/protocol choice, connection setup cost, preconnect/early hints
topics.takeaway: all three speak the same HTTP "language" (methods, headers, status codes). They differ in how requests share the wire: HTTP/1.1 = one at a time per connection, HTTP/2 = many at once over one TCP connection, HTTP/3 = many at once over QUIC, so one lost packet no longer stalls everything.

topics.title: DNS Resolution & CDN
topics.informs: CDN strategy, cache invalidation, global latency, preconnect/dns-prefetch, edge caching
topics.takeaway: DNS turns a name into the *nearest useful* address, and a CDN makes sure that address is physically close and already holds your bytes — together they decide how many milliseconds of pure distance every user pays before your app even starts.

topics.title: TCP/TLS Handshake
topics.informs: connection setup latency, preconnect, HTTPS/HSTS policy, critical-request sizing, mobile performance
topics.takeaway: before the first byte of HTML, a cold HTTPS visit pays DNS + TCP + TLS + request round trips. On a high-latency mobile link each round trip is expensive, so the winning moves are: fewer new connections, TLS 1.3 / QUIC, resumption, HSTS instead of redirects, and a small first response.

topics.title: REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC-Web
topics.informs: API contract choice, BFF, client caching, over-fetching, type generation
topics.takeaway: The choice is not "which is best" but "who controls the shape of the response, where does caching happen, and how are types shared". REST optimises for HTTP caching and simplicity, GraphQL for client-driven shape and fewer round trips, gRPC-Web/Connect for strict schemas and performance between typed services.

topics.title: WebSockets & SSE & Long Polling
topics.informs: real-time transport choice, reconnection strategy, live dashboards, chat, streaming AI responses
topics.takeaway: Use the simplest transport that fits the traffic direction. Server → client only (feeds, notifications, AI token streams) → SSE / streamed fetch. Frequent two-way messages (chat, collaboration, games) → WebSockets. Rare updates or hostile networks → polling. Whatever you choose, you own reconnection, ordering, auth and render batching.

topics.title: CORS & Same-Origin Policy
topics.informs: API/BFF topology, cookie & auth setup across domains, CDN/asset hosting, cross-origin isolation
topics.takeaway: SOP stops a page from *reading* cross-origin data. CORS is the server's opt-in that relaxes that rule for specific origins. It is enforced by the browser, protects users (not servers), and is not an authentication or CSRF defence.

topics.title: Service Workers & Web Workers
topics.informs: offline-first/PWA architecture, caching strategy, offloading heavy work (INP), update rollout
topics.takeaway: Web Workers move *computation* off the main thread; Service Workers move *network control* into your code. Both are separate threads with no DOM, talking to pages via messages.

topics.title: Web APIs (Intersection Observer, ResizeObserver)
topics.informs: lazy loading, infinite scroll, impression tracking, responsive components, RUM instrumentation
topics.takeaway: Don't ask the browser "where is it now?" on every scroll — ask it to tell you when something changes.

topics.title: Browser Caching Strategies
topics.informs: HTTP caching headers, asset versioning, CDN/edge cache policy, bfcache, repeat-visit performance
topics.takeaway: Cache aggressively what never changes (and rename it when it does); revalidate what can change; never store what must stay private.

sections.name: Header Decision Flowchart by Asset Type

topics.title: Client-Side Rendering (CSR)
topics.informs: rendering strategy per route, SEO and link previews, LCP vs TTFB trade-offs, JS bundle budgets, client routing and data-loading waterfalls, static hosting and SPA fallback, deploy version skew
topics.takeaway: CSR moves the work of building HTML from the server to the user's device: cheap to host and great for app-like interactivity, but the first view waits for JavaScript, and bots may see an empty page.

topics.title: Server-Side Rendering (SSR)
topics.informs: rendering strategy per route, TTFB vs FCP/LCP trade-offs, hydration cost and INP, SEO and link previews, personalization, CDN caching of HTML, server infrastructure and scaling, request-scoped state
topics.takeaway: SSR renders HTML on the server for every request: users and crawlers see real content immediately, but you pay with server work per request, a slower first byte, and a hydration step before the page is interactive.

topics.title: Static Site Generation (SSG)
topics.informs: rendering strategy per route, build time vs page count, content freshness and rebuild triggers, CDN hosting and atomic deploys, SEO for content sites, JS budget for content pages (zero-JS / islands), handling dynamic or personalized fragments on static pages
topics.takeaway: SSG renders pages once at build time and serves the same HTML files to everyone from a CDN: the fastest and cheapest delivery there is, as long as the content can be identical for all users and only as fresh as your last build.

topics.title: Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR)
topics.informs: rendering strategy per route, content freshness SLA, build time for large catalogs, CMS webhook → on-demand revalidation, CDN/origin load, self-hosted cache topology (shared cache handler), TTFB for content pages
topics.takeaway: ISR = static speed for every request, with pages rebuilt one at a time in the background — after a timer expires or when your CMS says so — instead of rebuilding the whole site.

topics.title: Streaming SSR & React Server Components
topics.informs: Suspense boundary placement, TTFB vs FCP/LCP trade-offs, client JS bundle size, server/client component split, data-fetching waterfalls, Server Actions security, proxy/CDN buffering config, SEO status codes under streaming
topics.takeaway: Streaming = don't make the fast parts wait for the slow parts. Server Components = don't send code to the browser for UI that never changes there.

topics.title: Island Architecture
topics.informs: framework choice for content-heavy sites (Astro, Fresh, Eleventy), JS budget and INP, hydration strategy per component (load / idle / visible / media / only), cross-island state sharing, MPA vs SPA navigation, server islands vs Partial Prerendering for personalized fragments
topics.takeaway: Islands = server-rendered static HTML as the default, with small, independent, individually hydrated interactive components — so you ship JavaScript only for the parts that need it.

topics.title: Edge Rendering
topics.informs: where SSR runs (edge vs regional vs origin), TTFB for global users, data locality and database placement, personalization and A/B testing at the CDN, middleware/proxy design, runtime choice (Edge vs Node.js)
topics.takeaway: Edge rendering wins only when the code AND the data it needs are close to the user. Compute near the user plus data far away = more long round trips, not fewer.

topics.title: Micro-Frontends Architecture
topics.informs: splitting a frontend across teams, composition strategy (build-time vs server vs edge vs client runtime), Module Federation vs import maps vs iframes, shared dependency and version policy, cross-app communication, CSS isolation, independent deployment and rollback
topics.takeaway: Micro-frontends split a frontend by team ownership so teams can ship independently. You buy organisational scale and pay with runtime overhead, duplication and coordination on shared contracts.

topics.title: Mono-repo vs Multi-repo
topics.informs: repository strategy for multiple apps and shared packages, design-system distribution, dependency and version policy, CI scale (affected builds, remote caching), release and versioning model, code ownership and module boundaries, how micro-frontends are organised in source control
topics.takeaway: A monorepo makes cross-project change cheap and keeps everyone on the same versions, but needs tooling to scale. A multi-repo makes isolation cheap, but every shared change becomes a versioned release that consumers must adopt.

topics.title: Component Architecture & Design Systems
topics.informs: component layering and folder boundaries, build vs adopt a UI library, headless vs styled components, design token pipeline, theming, design-system versioning and distribution, cross-framework component reuse, accessibility ownership
topics.takeaway: Components are how you split one app; a design system is how many teams and apps share the same building blocks, rules and language — consistently, accessibly and with versioned change.

topics.title: Feature-Sliced Design
topics.informs: folder structure for medium-to-large apps, module boundaries and import rules, where business logic lives, public APIs between modules, team ownership, lint-enforced architecture, onboarding speed
topics.takeaway: FSD sorts code by how business-specific it is (layers), then by business domain (slices), then by technical purpose (segments) — and only allows imports downward through each slice's public API.

topics.title: Module Bundling & Build Systems
topics.informs: bundler choice per framework, dev server and HMR speed, chunking and code-splitting strategy, tree shaking, browser targets and polyfills, source maps in production, environment variables and secrets, library packaging (ESM/CJS, exports), monorepo build orchestration and caching
topics.takeaway: A bundler turns a graph of source modules into a small number of optimised, cache-friendly files for the browser; a build system orchestrates and caches many such tasks across a codebase.

topics.title: Client State Management Patterns
topics.informs: where each piece of state lives (local, lifted, context, store, URL, server cache), choice of state library per stack, re-render cost and INP, SSR-safe stores, persistence and hydration, URL shareability
topics.takeaway: State management is mostly about deciding *where* each piece of state lives — and keeping as little of it as possible. The library is a secondary choice.

topics.title: Redux & Redux Toolkit
topics.informs: whether to adopt a centralized event-driven store, store and slice structure, async side-effect strategy (thunks, listeners, sagas), RTK Query vs a separate server-state library, normalized entity state, SSR store-per-request setup, migrating legacy Redux
topics.takeaway: Redux = one store, changed only by dispatching events that pure reducers turn into new state. Redux Toolkit is the official, required-in-practice way to write it today.

topics.title: Zustand / Jotai / Recoil
topics.informs: choosing a lightweight React state library (module store vs atomic), selector and re-render strategy, store-per-request SSR setup, persistence and hydration, migrating off Recoil, sharing state outside React
topics.takeaway: Zustand = small top-down stores with selectors. Jotai = bottom-up atoms with automatic dependency tracking. Recoil = the archived predecessor of the atomic model — migrate to Jotai (closest) or Zustand.

topics.title: Server State vs Client State
topics.informs: state ownership per data type, choice of data-fetching library vs global store, cache invalidation after mutations, URL vs store vs component state, SSR/RSC data hydration, duplicated-state bugs
topics.takeaway: Client state is owned by the UI and is always current. Server state is a cached snapshot of data someone else owns — treat it as a cache, not as your state.

topics.title: React Query / TanStack Query
topics.informs: server-state caching per resource (staleTime, gcTime), query-key design and invalidation strategy, mutation and optimistic-update flow, infinite lists and pagination, SSR/RSC prefetch and hydration, offline persistence, loading/error UX states
topics.takeaway: TanStack Query is an async state cache: give it a key and a function that returns a promise, and it handles caching, dedupe, background refetching, retries, invalidation and garbage collection for you.

topics.title: SWR & Stale-While-Revalidate
topics.informs: perceived latency vs freshness trade-off, `Cache-Control: stale-while-revalidate` at browser/CDN, Service Worker runtime caching strategy, choice between SWR and TanStack Query, revalidation triggers (focus, reconnect, polling), optimistic mutation flow, SSR fallback data
topics.takeaway: Stale-while-revalidate = respond from cache now, refresh in the background, update when the fresh copy arrives. It trades a short window of staleness for instant responses.

topics.title: GraphQL Client (Apollo, urql)
topics.informs: GraphQL client choice (Apollo vs urql vs Relay vs plain fetch + TanStack Query), normalized vs document cache, fetch/request policies, cache updates after mutations, fragment colocation, SSR hydration of GraphQL data, persisted queries, auth and subscription transport
topics.takeaway: A GraphQL client = transport + cache + framework bindings. The big decision is the cache: whole-response (document) caching is simple; normalized (per-entity) caching keeps every screen consistent but needs `id`s and update rules.

topics.title: Data Normalization & Caching
topics.informs: client cache shape (normalized entities vs per-query cache), entity identity and cache keys, invalidation strategy (TTL, tags, mutation-driven, push), staleTime/gcTime and memory limits, list and pagination storage, race and consistency handling, persisted caches and cross-tab sync
topics.takeaway: Store each thing once, point to it everywhere, and have an explicit rule for when each copy stops being trusted.

topics.title: Optimistic UI Updates
topics.informs: when to update optimistically vs wait for the server, rollback and reconciliation strategy, temporary IDs and idempotency keys, mutation ordering and race handling, pending/error UX and accessibility, offline mutation queues, library choice (React useOptimistic, TanStack Query, SWR, Apollo, urql, RTK Query)
topics.takeaway: Optimistic UI = predict the server's answer, show it instantly, and keep a reliable way to correct it. Use it when success is very likely and a brief wrong state is harmless.

topics.title: Pagination & Infinite Scroll
topics.informs: offset vs cursor API contract, numbered pages vs load more vs infinite scroll, list virtualization, scroll restoration, feed accessibility, SEO of listing pages, infinite-query cache design
topics.takeaway: Pick the API contract by data behaviour (offset for small/stable sets, cursors for big/live ones), pick the UI pattern by user intent (find vs browse), and virtualize whenever the DOM would otherwise grow without limit.

topics.title: Real-Time Data Sync
topics.informs: polling vs push-invalidate vs push-patch, merging live events into the query cache, event ordering and resync after reconnect, conflict resolution (LWW, OT, CRDT), presence, multi-tab connection sharing, rendering high-frequency updates
topics.takeaway: Real-time sync is not "open a WebSocket". It's a contract: a starting snapshot, an ordered stream of changes on top of it, a way to detect gaps and resync, and a rule for conflicting writes.

topics.title: Offline-First Architecture
topics.informs: online-only vs offline-capable vs offline-first scope, local database choice (IndexedDB, OPFS + SQLite), mutation outbox and idempotency, delta sync and tombstones, conflict resolution, storage quotas and eviction, PWA app shell, sync engine build vs buy
topics.takeaway: Offline-first means the UI only ever talks to local data; a separate sync process moves changes between that local data and the server whenever it can.

topics.title: Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS)
topics.informs: performance SLOs and alert thresholds, LCP element priority (preload, fetchpriority, SSR), main-thread budget per interaction, layout-stability rules (image dimensions, ad slots, font fallbacks), RUM instrumentation, rendering strategy per route
topics.takeaway: Core Web Vitals grade real users on three things: did the main content load fast (LCP ≤ 2.5 s), did the page respond quickly to every input (INP ≤ 200 ms), and did it stay visually stable (CLS ≤ 0.1), measured at the 75th percentile.

topics.title: Lighthouse & Performance Auditing
topics.informs: lab testing setup (device, network, throttling), CI performance gates (Lighthouse CI assertions), regression triage workflow, choosing between Lighthouse, DevTools, WebPageTest and RUM, interpreting the Performance score vs Core Web Vitals
topics.takeaway: Lighthouse is a reproducible lab test that explains *why* a page is slow and catches regressions before release; real-user data decides *whether* it is slow for your users.

topics.title: Performance Budgets
topics.informs: per-route JS/CSS/image byte limits, CI merge gates (size-limit, Lighthouse CI, bundler limits), third-party script governance, dependency selection, metric SLOs and RUM alerting, trade-off discussions between features and speed
topics.takeaway: A performance budget is an agreed limit (bytes, time or score) that protects a user-facing goal; it only works if it is derived from that goal, checked automatically on every change, and owned by someone who can say no.

topics.title: Code Splitting & Lazy Loading
topics.informs: initial JS budget per route, route-level vs component-level chunk boundaries, lazy-load trigger (route / interaction / viewport / idle), chunk prefetch policy, Suspense and loading-state design, vendor chunking for long-term caching, ChunkLoadError recovery after deploys, LCP / INP / TTI trade-offs
topics.takeaway: Ship the code for what the user is doing now; fetch the rest when (or just before) they need it — and never make them wait twice.

topics.title: Tree Shaking & Dead Code Elimination
topics.informs: dependency selection (ESM vs CommonJS, per-function imports), library packaging (`exports`, `sideEffects`, pure annotations), barrel-file policy, build-time flags and `NODE_ENV` stripping, bundler and minifier configuration, unused-code audits in CI, initial JS budget
topics.takeaway: Only code that is provably unused AND provably harmless to remove can be dropped. Your job is to make both facts easy for the tools to prove.

topics.title: Image Optimization
topics.informs: image format policy (AVIF / WebP / JPEG XL / SVG), responsive `srcset` / `sizes` and art direction, LCP image priority (`fetchpriority`, preload, never lazy), lazy-loading thresholds, CLS-safe sizing, image CDN vs build-time pipeline, placeholder strategy, caching of user uploads, GIF-to-video, alt-text and SVG security policy
topics.takeaway: Send the smallest file in the best format at the size it's displayed, reserve its space, load the hero first and everything else when it's about to be seen.

topics.title: Font Loading Strategies
topics.informs: font-display policy per font role, self-hosting vs third-party font services, font preloading, subsetting and unicode-range for i18n, variable vs static fonts, fallback metric overrides (CLS), text LCP, font caching headers
topics.takeaway: Show text immediately, make the fallback look like the real font, and fetch the real font early — or decide it isn't worth waiting for.

topics.title: Prefetching & Preloading
topics.informs: resource-hint strategy (preconnect, preload, modulepreload, prefetch), LCP resource discovery and fetchpriority, 103 Early Hints at the CDN, route and data prefetching in SPA routers, Speculation Rules prerendering for MPAs, bandwidth and server-load budgets for speculation, analytics on prerendered pages
topics.takeaway: Preload what *this* page certainly needs but finds late; prefetch or prerender what the *next* page probably needs — and only when the guess is good enough to pay for.

topics.title: JavaScript Bundle Optimization
topics.informs: JS budget per route, dependency selection and replacement, browser targets and polyfill policy, chunking and long-term caching, minification and Brotli/zstd compression, script loading attributes, third-party script governance, hydration cost and "less JS" architectures, bundle-size checks in CI
topics.takeaway: The fastest JavaScript is the JavaScript you don't ship. Measure it, delete it, replace it, split it, shrink it, cache it — in that order.

topics.title: Virtual Scrolling & Windowing
topics.informs: list virtualization vs pagination vs content-visibility, DOM size budget, fixed vs measured row heights, overscan, scroll restoration, accessibility of long lists and grids, find-in-page trade-offs, table/grid/chat/feed architecture
topics.takeaway: Windowing renders a constant number of rows no matter how long the list is — the DOM cost depends on the viewport size, not on the data size.

topics.title: React Performance (memo, useMemo, useCallback)
topics.informs: when to memoize vs restructure components, React Compiler adoption, context and store design (selectors, split contexts), INP of typing and filtering, list row rendering cost, profiling workflow, equivalent strategies in Vue/Angular/Svelte
topics.takeaway: Re-renders are normal and usually cheap. Memoize only what profiling proves is slow — and prefer restructuring (or the React Compiler) over sprinkling `memo` everywhere.

topics.title: Debouncing & Throttling
topics.informs: search-as-you-type and autocomplete request strategy, autosave design, scroll/resize/pointer handling, rAF batching, request cancellation and race conditions, client-side rate limiting, INP of high-frequency events, framework hooks and RxJS operators
topics.takeaway: Debounce runs once after the burst ends; throttle runs at a steady maximum rate during the burst. Pick by asking: "Do I need the final value, or regular updates while it's happening?"

topics.title: Web Workers for Heavy Computation
topics.informs: what to move off the main thread (INP, long tasks), worker topology (one-shot vs stateful vs pool), message protocol and cancellation design, data format across threads (clone vs transfer vs SharedArrayBuffer), COOP/COEP headers for shared memory and WASM threads, bundler/framework worker setup
topics.takeaway: Workers keep the waiter free. They pay off only when the cooking is long and the hatch traffic is small: move computation, not data.

topics.title: Memory Leaks in Frontend Apps
topics.informs: component lifecycle and cleanup contracts, subscription/listener/timer ownership, bounded client caches (LRU/TTL, gcTime), long-lived SPA sessions and dashboards, third-party widget teardown, leak testing in CI (MemLab), memory monitoring in RUM
topics.takeaway: Garbage collection frees what is unreachable, not what is unused. A leak is anything you no longer need that is still reachable — so every subscription you start needs an owner who ends it.

topics.title: Animation Performance (CSS vs JS)
topics.informs: animation technology per use case (CSS transitions/keyframes, Web Animations API, rAF/JS libraries, canvas/WebGL), compositor-friendly property choice, will-change and layer budget, scroll-driven animations and View Transitions adoption, prefers-reduced-motion policy, animation impact on INP/CLS/LCP, motion library choice per framework
topics.takeaway: Animate `transform` and `opacity`, let the browser run the animation (CSS or the Web Animations API), and use frame-by-frame JS only when you need physics, gestures or logic per frame. Always respect reduced-motion preferences.

topics.title: Atomic Design Methodology
topics.informs: component granularity and layering, design-system folder and package structure, Storybook and Figma library taxonomy, where data and state enter the component tree, testing strategy per layer, shared vocabulary between design and engineering
topics.takeaway: Atomic Design is a vocabulary for building UIs from the smallest parts up, while always checking those parts in real, full-page context. It's a mental model, not a folder structure you must copy.

topics.title: Design Tokens
topics.informs: token tiers and naming, single source of truth between Figma and code, theming and dark mode architecture, multi-brand support, token build pipeline (DTCG + Style Dictionary), CSS custom properties vs build-time constants, cross-platform (web, iOS, Android) consistency, design-system versioning
topics.takeaway: Design tokens are named design decisions — colours, spacing, type, motion — stored once in a platform-neutral file and generated into every platform's code, so design and every app stay in sync and themes become a mapping change, not a code change.

topics.title: Component API Design
topics.informs: prop naming and typing conventions, variants vs booleans, composition vs configuration, controlled vs uncontrolled support, native attribute and ref forwarding, polymorphism (`as` / `asChild`), styling hooks (className, CSS variables, data attributes), accessibility enforced by types, breaking-change policy and deprecation of props
topics.takeaway: A component API is a promise to every developer who uses it. Keep it small, consistent with the platform and the rest of your library, typed so wrong usage doesn't compile, open for composition, and change it only through a deprecation path.

topics.title: Compound Component Pattern
topics.informs: component API shape (composition vs configuration props), design-system primitives (Tabs, Select, Menu, Accordion, Dialog), implicit shared state via context / provide-inject / DI, ARIA pattern wiring, RSC client boundaries, tree-shaking of component parts
topics.takeaway: a compound component is a small family of components that share hidden state through the parent, so the caller controls structure and content while the library controls behaviour.

topics.title: Headless UI / Renderless Components
topics.informs: build vs adopt a behaviour layer for a design system, headless library choice per framework, accessibility ownership (keyboard, focus, ARIA), styling strategy (data attributes, render-state classes), cross-framework component reuse, copy-in (shadcn/ui) vs dependency, bundle and upgrade cost
topics.takeaway: headless components give you the hard, invisible part (behaviour + accessibility) and let you own the visible part (markup + styles) completely.

topics.title: Controlled vs Uncontrolled Components
topics.informs: form architecture (FormData and actions vs field-level state), form library choice, design-system prop contracts (value/defaultValue/onValueChange, open/defaultOpen/onOpenChange), validation timing, per-keystroke re-render cost, state reset strategy, URL- or store-synced component state
topics.takeaway: controlled = the parent owns the value and the component just reports changes; uncontrolled = the component (or the DOM) owns the value and the parent reads it when needed.

topics.title: Higher-Order Components & Render Props
topics.informs: logic-reuse pattern choice (HOC vs render prop vs hook), migrating legacy HOC/render-prop code, design-system extension points (renderItem, slots, render-state props), cross-cutting concerns (auth guards, error boundaries, feature flags), TypeScript typing of wrappers, ref forwarding, cross-framework equivalents (scoped slots, snippets, ng-template)
topics.takeaway: HOCs wrap a component to inject behavior; render props hand behavior to a function you supply. Hooks now do the logic-sharing job for most code, but render props are still the best way for a component to let callers control rendering.

topics.title: Custom Hooks Patterns
topics.informs: logic-reuse architecture, headless design-system APIs (prop getters, state reducers), syncing with browser APIs and external stores (useSyncExternalStore), data-fetching layer choice, SSR/RSC safety of client logic, hook API shape (tuple vs object, stable references), hook testing strategy, cross-framework equivalents (composables, signals, runes)
topics.takeaway: A custom hook is a function whose name starts with `use` and that calls other hooks. It lets components share stateful logic — each call gets its own independent state.

sections.name: Should This Be a Custom Hook?

topics.title: Storybook & Component Documentation
topics.informs: component workshop and docs tooling choice, story coverage per component state, design-system documentation structure, component testing strategy (interaction, a11y, visual regression), CI for UI libraries, design-to-code handoff, mocking data and network for isolated components, multi-framework and native-mobile component catalogs
topics.takeaway: Storybook renders each component state in isolation as a "story". Those stories become living documentation, a review surface for designers, and test cases — one artifact, three uses.

topics.title: CSS Architecture (CSS-in-JS, Tailwind, CSS Modules)
topics.informs: styling approach per app or design system, CSS scoping strategy, runtime vs build-time styling cost, React Server Components compatibility, cascade layer ordering, CSS bundle size and critical CSS, how a component library ships its styles
topics.takeaway: Every CSS architecture answers the same three questions: how do I avoid name collisions, how do I control which rule wins, and how do I delete CSS safely?

topics.title: Responsive Design Patterns
topics.informs: breakpoint strategy and tokens, media vs container queries per component, fluid typography and spacing, responsive images and LCP, navigation and table patterns on small screens, SSR-safe viewport logic, touch target sizing, mobile viewport units and safe areas, WCAG reflow compliance
topics.takeaway: Design for the content and the container first; use viewport breakpoints only where the whole page layout genuinely needs to change.

topics.title: Theming & Dark Mode
topics.informs: theme token architecture (primitive vs semantic), CSS custom properties vs JS theme providers, light/dark/system preference model, flash-free theme loading with SSR and CSP, theme preference persistence, dark palette and contrast design, forced-colors support, multi-brand and white-label theming, native-platform dark mode
topics.takeaway: Components reference roles (`--color-surface`), themes assign values to those roles, and the right theme must be applied before the first paint.

topics.title: ARIA Roles, States & Properties
topics.informs: native HTML vs ARIA per widget, accessible names for icon buttons, custom widget contracts (tabs, disclosure, combobox), live-region announcements, hiding strategy (aria-hidden vs inert), design-system component a11y APIs, choosing headless UI libraries
topics.takeaway: ARIA only changes what assistive technology is *told* — never how the element *behaves*. Use native HTML first; add ARIA only to describe custom widgets you have fully built yourself.

topics.title: Keyboard Navigation & Focus Management
topics.informs: focus strategy on SPA route changes, modal/drawer/popover focus handling, roving tabindex vs aria-activedescendant in composite widgets, focus-ring design tokens, keyboard shortcut policy, skip links, sticky-header focus obscuring, design-system keyboard contracts
topics.takeaway: Everything a mouse can do, the keyboard must do too — and whenever the UI changes, *you* decide where focus goes next, because the browser often can't.

topics.title: Screen Reader Testing
topics.informs: screen reader + browser support matrix, manual a11y QA in the definition of done, release test scripts for custom widgets, automated screen reader tests (Guidepup), a11y bug triage and reporting, when to test with disabled users, native mobile (VoiceOver/TalkBack) QA
topics.takeaway: Automated tools check the markup; only a real screen reader shows whether the experience works. Test the key journeys with the screen reader + browser pairs your users actually use.

topics.title: Color Contrast & Visual Accessibility
topics.informs: color token pairs and palette design, text/UI contrast thresholds (WCAG 1.4.3, 1.4.11), focus-ring design, status/error/link styling without color-only cues, dark mode and high-contrast themes, forced-colors (Windows Contrast themes) support, zoom/reflow/text-spacing resilience, reduced-motion policy, data-viz palettes
topics.takeaway: Every piece of meaning on screen must survive low contrast eyesight, no color perception, zoom, and the user's own color settings — measure it, don't eyeball it.

topics.title: Accessible Forms & Error Handling
topics.informs: form field component API (label, hint, error wiring), validation timing (submit vs blur vs input), native vs custom validation, error summary and focus strategy, live-region announcements for async results, server validation error contract, autocomplete and authentication UX, session-timeout handling, multi-step form design
topics.takeaway: Every field needs a visible label, every error needs words (not just red), and after a failed submit the user must be taken straight to a list of what to fix.

topics.title: Automated A11y Testing (axe, Lighthouse)
topics.informs: a11y tooling per pipeline stage (lint, unit, Storybook, E2E, Lighthouse CI, monitoring), axe rule tags and WCAG level targeting, CI gate thresholds and baselines for legacy apps, what still needs manual and screen-reader testing, Lighthouse accessibility score interpretation, design-system a11y test coverage, native mobile accessibility audits
topics.takeaway: Automated tools reliably find a meaningful share of accessibility bugs, cheaply and early — run them everywhere — but a clean report is the start of testing, not proof of accessibility.

topics.title: Internationalization (i18n) Architecture
topics.informs: locale negotiation and persistence, localized URL strategy and hreflang SEO, message format (ICU) and key strategy, translation catalog loading and code splitting, SSR/SSG per locale and hydration safety, translation pipeline (TMS, CI checks, pseudo-localization), i18n library choice per framework, server API contract for localized content
topics.takeaway: Internationalization is designing the app so that language and regional conventions are data, chosen per request — localization is then just supplying that data.

topics.title: RTL Layout Support
topics.informs: document direction (`<html dir>`) per locale, CSS logical properties as a design-system rule, icon mirroring policy, bidi-safe rendering of user-generated content (`dir="auto"`, `<bdi>`), direction-aware JS (scroll, keyboard, gestures, positioning), RTL support in component libraries and native apps, RTL visual regression testing
topics.takeaway: Build layouts with *start* and *end*, never *left* and *right* — then right-to-left is a setting, not a second codebase. Mirror what shows direction; never mirror what doesn't.

topics.title: Date, Number & Currency Formatting
topics.informs: Intl API usage and formatter caching, date/time data model (instant vs zoned vs plain date), time zone handling and SSR hydration safety, money representation (minor units + ISO 4217) in APIs and state, Temporal adoption and polyfills, date-library choice (Moment migration), localized number/date input parsing, per-framework formatting (pipes, filters, FormatStyle)
topics.takeaway: Store values in a neutral, exact form (UTC instants, plain dates, integer minor units + currency code) and format them at the edge with `Intl` for the viewer's locale and time zone. Never build formatted strings by hand.

topics.title: XSS Prevention (Reflected, Stored, DOM)
topics.informs: rendering of user-generated content, rich-text and Markdown pipelines, escape-hatch policy (`dangerouslySetInnerHTML` / `v-html` / `{@html}`), URL validation, Trusted Types and CSP rollout, auth token storage (HttpOnly cookie vs localStorage), user-upload hosting domain, SSR state serialization
topics.takeaway: XSS happens when data crosses into a code context. Keep data as data — encode it for the exact context it lands in, sanitize HTML you must render, and add CSP + Trusted Types so a single mistake isn't fatal.

topics.title: Content Security Policy (CSP)
topics.informs: security headers at the edge/server, nonce vs hash strategy per rendering mode (SSR vs static/CDN), HTML cacheability, third-party script and tag-manager policy, CSS-in-JS and inline-style choices, Trusted Types rollout, clickjacking protection (`frame-ancestors`), violation reporting pipeline
topics.takeaway: CSP is a browser-enforced allow-list for what a page may execute and load. A strict, nonce- or hash-based CSP turns most XSS bugs from "attacker runs code" into "blocked and reported" — but it's a second layer, not a substitute for output encoding.

topics.title: CSRF Protection
topics.informs: cookie-based session and BFF design, `SameSite` cookie settings, API/app domain topology (same-site vs cross-site), CSRF token strategy (synchronizer vs signed double-submit vs Fetch Metadata), HTTP method semantics, WebSocket handshake checks, GraphQL endpoint hardening, framework CSRF configuration
topics.takeaway: CSRF abuses credentials the browser attaches automatically (cookies). Reject cross-site state-changing requests — `SameSite` cookies plus a `Sec-Fetch-Site`/`Origin` check, or tokens — and never change state on `GET`.

topics.title: Authentication Flows in SPAs
topics.informs: login architecture (session cookie vs tokens vs BFF), OAuth/OIDC flow choice, PKCE, token refresh strategy, route guards, logout and multi-tab sync, SSO and passkeys, native-app login
topics.takeaway: An SPA cannot keep a secret. Pick a flow where the browser holds as little as possible — ideally just an `HttpOnly` session cookie — and let the server do the trusted work.

topics.title: Secure Token Storage
topics.informs: where to keep session IDs, access and refresh tokens (cookie vs memory vs Web Storage vs worker), cookie attributes and prefixes, token lifetimes, sender-constrained tokens (DPoP), mobile secure storage, token leakage via logs and URLs
topics.takeaway: No browser storage is safe from XSS. Choose the option that stops the credential from being *stolen and reused elsewhere*, keep it short-lived, and prevent XSS in the first place.

topics.title: Subresource Integrity (SRI)
topics.informs: third-party script and CDN loading policy, self-hosting vs public CDNs, build-time integrity hashes, `crossorigin` and CORS setup, Integrity-Policy enforcement, import maps, supply-chain incident response
topics.takeaway: SRI pins a resource to exact bytes: the browser refuses anything else. Use it for versioned files you don't control; self-host when you can.

topics.title: Clickjacking & iframe Protection
topics.informs: frame-ancestors / X-Frame-Options policy per route, embeddable widget design, third-party iframe sandboxing, postMessage contracts, confirmation UX for sensitive actions, cookie SameSite policy
topics.takeaway: Clickjacking tricks a user into clicking a real, logged-in page hidden inside an attacker's frame. Stop it with `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors` (plus `X-Frame-Options` for old clients); sandbox every frame you embed.

topics.title: Dependency Vulnerability Scanning
topics.informs: CI security gates, dependency update policy (Dependabot/Renovate), lockfile and install-script hardening, package manager choice, SBOM generation, vulnerability triage SLAs, third-party library selection
topics.takeaway: Know exactly what you ship (lockfile, SBOM), check it continuously against advisories, triage by real exposure, update on a steady cadence — and treat install-time code from strangers as the dangerous part.

topics.title: Unit Testing Components (Jest, Vitest)
topics.informs: test runner choice (Jest vs Vitest vs framework CLI), DOM environment (jsdom, happy-dom, real browser), mocking boundaries, fake timers, snapshot policy, coverage thresholds, test file layout, CI sharding, testability of component APIs
topics.takeaway: A unit test checks one component or function in isolation, fast, with controlled inputs — props, events, mocked dependencies — and asserts on what the user or caller would observe.

topics.title: React Testing Library Patterns
topics.informs: component test strategy, query and selector conventions (role-first vs test IDs), accessible markup as a testability requirement, async UI testing, network mocking boundary (MSW), test-utils and provider setup, hook testing, Enzyme and react-test-renderer migration, cross-framework component testing (Vue, Angular, Svelte, React Native)
topics.takeaway: Test what the user sees and does, not how the component is built. If a refactor keeps the UI the same, the tests should keep passing.

topics.title: Integration Testing
topics.informs: test boundary and mocking policy (what is real vs faked), network mocking with MSW, mock-vs-API drift and contract testing, feature- and route-level test design, test data factories, jsdom vs real-browser test environment, CI stage layout for integration suites, cross-framework integration patterns (Vue, Angular, Svelte, React Native, Flutter)
topics.takeaway: An integration test runs your real components, state and data code together and fakes only what's outside your app: the network, time and third-party services.

topics.title: E2E Testing (Playwright, Cypress)
topics.informs: E2E tool choice (Playwright vs Cypress vs WebDriver-based), which user journeys get E2E coverage, cross-browser test matrix, locator conventions, auth and test-data strategy, real vs mocked backend in E2E, flaky-test policy, CI sharding and artifacts, preview-deployment gating, native mobile E2E tooling (Detox, Maestro, Appium, XCUITest, Espresso)
topics.takeaway: E2E tests prove that the critical user journeys work in a real browser against the real system. Keep them few, focused on what matters most, and free of fixed waits.

topics.title: Visual Regression Testing
topics.informs: UI regression gates in CI, design-system release safety, choosing self-hosted vs hosted screenshot tooling, baseline storage and review workflow, snapshot matrix (browsers, viewports, themes, locales), flake control (fonts, animations, time, data), CI rendering environment (Docker)
topics.takeaway: Visual regression testing compares screenshots against approved baselines so CSS and layout bugs that no assertion would catch get seen by a human before users see them.

topics.title: Performance Testing
topics.informs: CI performance regression gates, lab test environment (CPU/network throttling, dedicated runners), statistical base-vs-head comparison, interaction latency tests for INP, load testing SSR/BFF/edge before launches, microbenchmarks for hot code paths, memory-leak tests, mobile startup benchmarks
topics.takeaway: Performance testing turns "it feels slower" into a repeatable, statistically sound check that runs before users notice — across page loads, interactions, servers and memory.

topics.title: Accessibility Testing
topics.informs: layered a11y test strategy (lint, component, E2E, manual, assistive tech), CI accessibility gates and baselines, WCAG 2.2 AA conformance evidence, screen reader and browser test matrix, design-system a11y contracts, release sign-off and audit cadence, native mobile accessibility checks
topics.takeaway: Automated a11y tests catch the measurable problems cheaply on every commit; only humans using keyboards, screen readers and zoom can confirm that the experience actually works.

topics.title: Testing Strategies & Pyramid
topics.informs: test mix per layer (unit/integration/E2E), mocking boundaries, CI pipeline stages and time budget, flaky-test policy, coverage targets, release confidence and shift-right monitoring
topics.takeaway: A testing strategy is a budget: spend it on the cheapest test that gives real confidence about a behavior — many fast checks at the bottom, a few realistic journeys at the top, and monitoring after release.

topics.title: Error Boundaries & Global Error Handling
topics.informs: error boundary placement and granularity, fallback UX and recovery, global error/unhandledrejection handlers, API error model, chunk-load recovery, error reporting pipeline, SSR/RSC error handling
topics.takeaway: Contain errors close to where they happen, give the user a way to recover, and make sure nothing escapes without being reported.

topics.title: Error Tracking (Sentry, Datadog RUM)
topics.informs: error-tracking vendor choice, SDK initialization and bundle cost, source map and release pipeline, issue grouping and alerting, error sampling vs session sampling, PII scrubbing and consent, frontend-to-backend trace correlation, ad-blocker resilience
topics.takeaway: An error tracker turns millions of raw, minified crash reports into a short, de-minified, prioritized list of issues — each with the context needed to fix it and an owner to fix it.

topics.title: Real User Monitoring (RUM)
topics.informs: RUM pipeline design (collect, beacon, ingest, aggregate), which browser timing APIs to collect, session sampling rate, segmentation dimensions and cardinality, percentile dashboards and field SLOs, release-regression alerting, frontend-to-backend trace correlation, telemetry privacy and consent, vendor vs self-hosted RUM
topics.takeaway: RUM measures what real users actually experienced, on their devices and networks, and only becomes useful once you segment it and look at percentiles instead of averages.

topics.title: Synthetic Monitoring
topics.informs: uptime and availability SLOs, which user journeys to script as browser checks, check frequency and location count vs cost, alert quorum and retry policy, post-deploy smoke gates, scheduled lab performance tracking, private locations for internal apps, test accounts and synthetic-traffic tagging, synthetic vs RUM coverage
topics.takeaway: synthetic monitoring runs the same scripted visit on a schedule from known places, so you find outages and regressions before users do, even when there is no traffic.

topics.title: Feature Flags & A/B Testing
topics.informs: decoupling deploy from release, flag types and lifetimes, client vs server vs edge flag evaluation, flicker-free variant rendering, CDN caching with variants, percentage rollouts and kill switches, experiment design (randomization unit, sample size, guardrails), exposure logging, flag cleanup and technical debt, vendor vs OpenFeature vs in-house
topics.takeaway: flags let you ship code dark and turn it on gradually or off instantly; A/B tests use random flag assignment plus careful statistics to learn whether a change actually helped.

topics.title: Analytics Architecture
topics.informs: event taxonomy and tracking plan, analytics SDK facade vs direct vendor calls, client-side vs server-side collection, CDP build vs buy, consent gating, identity stitching, SPA page-view tracking, beacon transport and batching, third-party script budget (INP), ad-blocker resilience, data quality checks in CI
topics.takeaway: Analytics architecture = a well-defined rulebook for events, a thin client that records them cheaply and only with consent, and a pipeline that delivers clean, deduplicated data to every tool that needs it.

topics.title: Logging Best Practices
topics.informs: client log levels per environment, structured log schema, frontend-to-backend correlation (trace context, request IDs), breadcrumb ring buffer vs shipped logs, log sampling and rate limits, PII redaction, console stripping in production builds, Reporting API (CSP, deprecations), SSR logging, observability vendor choice
topics.takeaway: Frontend logging = structured, levelled events with enough context to correlate with the backend, sent sparingly from devices you don't control, and scrubbed of anything private.

topics.title: Progressive Web Apps (PWA)
topics.informs: PWA vs native vs hybrid choice, web app manifest design (id, scope, icons, display), install UX per platform, offline scope and app shell, service worker update UX, Web Push and notification strategy (incl. iOS limits), app-store distribution (TWA, Microsoft Store), storage persistence, standalone-mode UI (safe areas, navigation)
topics.takeaway: A PWA is a normal website that adds a manifest, a service worker and app-quality UX, so it can be installed, work offline and use some device features — while staying a URL that's always one click away.

topics.title: WebAssembly (WASM) in Frontend
topics.informs: WASM vs JS vs server for a CPU-heavy feature, source language and toolchain choice, JS-WASM boundary design (batching, memory sharing), worker placement, .wasm loading and caching (streaming compile, MIME type, preload), CSP `wasm-unsafe-eval`, COOP/COEP for WASM threads, bundle-size budgets, framework, SSR and edge integration
topics.takeaway: WebAssembly is a fast, sandboxed compute engine next to JavaScript, not a replacement for it. Use it for heavy, self-contained work you can hand over in big batches, and keep the UI in JS.

topics.title: Web Components & Shadow DOM
topics.informs: framework-agnostic design systems, embeddable third-party widgets, micro-frontend integration contracts, style encapsulation vs theming (custom properties, `::part`), component API shape (attributes vs properties vs events), form participation and accessibility of custom controls, SSR with Declarative Shadow DOM, choosing Lit/Stencil vs framework components
topics.takeaway: Web Components are framework-independent, browser-native components: a custom tag (Custom Elements) with a private inside (Shadow DOM), a public API made of attributes, properties, events, slots, and styling hooks.

topics.title: Authentication Architecture (BFF Pattern)
topics.informs: BFF vs token-mediating backend vs browser OAuth client, where OAuth tokens live, session store design (server-side vs sealed cookie), session cookie attributes, CSRF defense for cookie-authenticated APIs, token refresh concurrency across BFF instances, API proxying and downstream token exchange, login/logout endpoints (RP-initiated and back-channel logout), deployment topology (same-origin routing, CDN rules), SSR framework integration
topics.takeaway: A BFF keeps OAuth tokens on the server and gives the browser only a same-site, `HttpOnly` session cookie. It removes token theft from the threat model, at the cost of running a server and defending against CSRF.

topics.title: SEO for SPAs & Dynamic Content
topics.informs: rendering strategy per route (CSR vs SSR/SSG/ISR) for indexable pages, URL and routing design (History API vs hash), HTTP status codes and soft 404s in SPAs, metadata/Open Graph/structured data pipeline, sitemaps and robots policy, link previews for social and AI crawlers, infinite scroll and faceted navigation crawlability
topics.takeaway: Put everything a crawler needs — content, links, metadata and the correct status code — into the HTML the server sends. JavaScript may improve the page; it should not be required to understand it.

topics.title: Deployment & CI/CD for Frontend
topics.informs: CI pipeline stages and quality gates, hosting model (static CDN vs SSR server vs serverless/edge), build-once-deploy-many and environment config, atomic deploys and asset upload order, version skew handling, preview environments, canary/blue-green/feature-flag release strategy, rollback design, pipeline security (OIDC, pinned actions), source maps and release tracking
topics.takeaway: Make every change small, tested and built once; ship the same artifact everywhere; switch traffic atomically; watch real users; and keep the previous version one click away.

topics.title: CDN Architecture & Edge Caching
topics.informs: CDN cache key design, edge vs browser TTL policy, tiered caching and origin shielding, purge and invalidation architecture (tags, soft purge, event-driven), caching HTML/SSR/API responses, personalization at the edge, edge compute placement and edge data consistency, origin protection and signed URLs, cache poisoning and deception defenses, CDN observability (Cache-Status, hit ratio)
topics.takeaway: The edge is a shared, distributed cache with programmable logic. Design the key so identical things match and different things never collide, decide freshness explicitly, invalidate by meaning (tags), and never let anything personal into a shared entry.

topics.title: Monorepo Tooling (Turborepo, Nx)
topics.informs: monorepo task runner choice (Turborepo vs Nx vs Bazel/Rush/moon), CI duration and affected-only builds, cache-key correctness (inputs, outputs, env vars), remote cache hosting and cache-poisoning risk, module boundary enforcement, code generation and automated migrations, Docker images for one app out of many
topics.takeaway: A monorepo tool is a smart head chef: it knows what depends on what, never cooks the same thing twice, and only cooks what changed. Its labels (cache keys) must list every ingredient, or it serves the wrong dish.

topics.title: Design a News Feed (Facebook/Twitter)
topics.informs: feed rendering strategy (SSR first page vs CSR), cursor pagination and infinite scroll, list virtualization with variable heights, normalized post/user cache, optimistic reactions and posting, real-time "new posts" delivery (SSE/WebSocket/polling), media loading and CLS, feed accessibility (`role="feed"`), user-generated content security, offline drafts
topics.takeaway: A news feed is a never-ending, personalised list: load it in cursor-based pages, render only what's visible, store each entity once, respond to taps instantly, and never move content under the reader's eyes.

topics.title: Design an Autocomplete / Typeahead
topics.informs: client-side vs server-side suggestion filtering, debounce interval and minimum query length, request cancellation and race handling, suggestion caching (in-memory LRU, HTTP cache, prefix reuse), WAI-ARIA combobox semantics and keyboard model, IME composition and Unicode normalization, safe match highlighting, reusable headless component API
topics.takeaway: An autocomplete is a race between the user's typing and the network: wait for pauses, cancel what's outdated, remember what you've seen, and let keyboard and screen-reader users drive it exactly like mouse users.

topics.title: Design an Image Carousel / Gallery
topics.informs: carousel engine choice (CSS scroll-snap vs JS transform), image loading priority and LCP, srcset/sizes and image CDN variants, autoplay and WCAG 2.2.2 compliance, carousel ARIA pattern, lightbox dialog and focus management, URL state for deep-linked photos, gallery pagination and virtualization, CLS-safe placeholders
topics.takeaway: show the first image fast, load the others just before they're needed, let the user control the motion, and make every action work with a keyboard, a screen reader and a thumb.

topics.title: Design a Chat Application UI
topics.informs: real-time transport choice (WebSocket vs SSE vs polling), reconnect and resync strategy, optimistic sends and idempotency keys, message ordering and deduplication, reverse infinite scroll and scroll anchoring, message-list virtualization, offline outbox, multi-tab socket sharing, notifications and unread badges, chat accessibility (role=log, composer, IME), bidi text, XSS-safe message rendering, WebSocket authentication
topics.takeaway: a chat client is a local, ordered, deduplicated copy of the server's message log, kept in sync over an unreliable real-time connection, rendered as a bottom-anchored virtual list.

topics.title: Design a Spreadsheet (Google Sheets)
topics.informs: DOM virtualization vs canvas rendering for large grids, sparse cell storage and style interning, variable row/column sizes (prefix sums), formula parsing and dependency-graph recalculation, moving computation to Web Workers, collaborative editing (server-ordered ops, OT vs CRDT), undo/redo with commands, ARIA grid pattern for virtualized grids, clipboard interop, locale-aware number parsing, CSV/formula injection
topics.takeaway: store only non-empty cells, draw only the visible ones, recalculate only what depends on the change (off the main thread), and let a server order everyone's edits.

topics.title: Design a Video Player (YouTube)
topics.informs: adaptive bitrate streaming (HLS/DASH via MSE or native), player state machine, watch-page rendering strategy, startup time and rebuffering, poster/LCP and CLS, captions and media accessibility, DRM (EME) and signed URLs, QoE analytics, ad insertion (CSAI vs SSAI), persistent mini-player across SPA navigation
topics.takeaway: a modern web video player is a small streaming client: it reads a manifest, downloads short segments at a quality chosen from bandwidth and buffer health, feeds them into the `<video>` element, and wraps all of it in an accessible, keyboard-friendly control layer.

topics.title: Design a Drag-and-Drop Board (Trello)
topics.informs: drag-and-drop library choice (native HTML DnD vs pointer events), ordering strategy (fractional positions vs indexes), optimistic move with rollback, real-time board sync and conflict handling, normalized board state, keyboard and screen-reader drag alternatives (WCAG 2.5.7), drag performance and auto-scroll, list virtualization
topics.takeaway: a Trello-style board is a pointer/keyboard interaction engine on top of normalized, fractionally ordered data. Moves are applied optimistically, sent as a single small update, and broadcast to other viewers in real time, with an accessible non-drag way to do the same move.

topics.title: Design a Rich Text Editor
topics.informs: editor architecture (contenteditable + document model vs custom rendering), editor library choice (ProseMirror/Tiptap, Lexical, Slate, Quill, CKEditor), document schema and storage format, `beforeinput`/IME handling, undo/redo, paste sanitization and XSS, real-time collaboration (OT vs CRDT/Yjs), autosave and versioning, toolbar and editor accessibility, large-document performance
topics.takeaway: a production rich text editor treats the DOM as a *view*. User input is turned into commands/transactions on a schema-validated document model, which is the single source of truth for rendering, undo, collaboration, storage and sanitization.

topics.title: Design an E-Commerce Product Page
topics.informs: rendering strategy per data freshness (catalog vs price vs stock vs personalization), CDN cache keys and tag-based invalidation, LCP hero image strategy, variant selection and URL state, add-to-cart mutation and idempotency, SEO structured data and canonical URLs, third-party script budget, money formatting and multi-market pricing
topics.takeaway: A product page is several pages glued together, each with a different freshness and audience: cache the shared parts hard, fetch the volatile and personal parts separately, and let the server stay the source of truth for price and stock.

topics.title: Design a Dashboard with Real-Time Data
topics.informs: real-time transport choice (polling vs SSE vs WebSocket), snapshot + delta sync and gap recovery, update batching and render throttling, chart rendering technology (SVG vs Canvas vs WebGL), time-series memory bounds and downsampling, Web Worker offloading, multi-tab connection sharing, accessible live charts, dashboard layout persistence
topics.takeaway: A real-time dashboard is a snapshot plus a stream of deltas, merged into a bounded store, and painted at a human pace — not a re-render per message.

topics.title: Design a Multi-Step Form / Wizard
topics.informs: wizard state machine and conditional (branching) steps, URL-per-step routing and Back-button behavior, per-step vs final validation and shared client/server schemas, draft autosave and resume (server vs browser storage for PII), submit idempotency and server error mapping to steps, focus management and progress semantics, form schema versioning, funnel analytics without PII
topics.takeaway: A wizard is a state machine over a single draft: validate each step locally, persist the draft safely, re-validate everything on the server at submit, and never lose the user's answers or their place.

topics.title: Design a Notification System UI
topics.informs: real-time transport for notifications (SSE vs WebSocket vs polling), one connection per browser (cross-tab leader election), unread-count ownership and "seen vs read" semantics, cursor pagination of the inbox, optimistic mark-as-read, toast queueing and timing, Web Push and permission-prompt UX, live-region accessibility, notification grouping and i18n plurals, XSS-safe notification templates
topics.takeaway: A notification system UI is three channels (inbox, toast, push) fed by one event stream, with a server-owned unread count, careful permission UX, and accessible, polite announcements.

topics.title: Design a Map-Based Application
topics.informs: map library choice (Leaflet vs MapLibre GL vs Google Maps vs OpenLayers), raster vs vector tiles, viewport-driven data fetching (bbox, tile-keyed caching), marker strategy (DOM markers vs GL layers vs clustering), list–map synchronization, URL state for shareable views, geolocation permission UX, map accessibility (keyboard, dragging alternatives, list equivalent), lazy-loading the map and LCP, API-key and tile-usage policy, label language and RTL text
topics.takeaway: A map app is a camera over a tiled world: fetch only what the viewport needs, draw markers on the GPU or cluster them, keep the list and URL in sync with the camera, and always offer a non-map way to get the same information.

topics.title: Design a Calendar Component
topics.informs: date/time representation (instant + IANA zone vs floating all-day dates), Temporal vs Date libraries, DST-safe day/week math, recurring events (RRULE expansion, exceptions, this/following/all edits), overlapping-event layout algorithm, range-based fetching and prefetching of adjacent periods, drag-to-move/resize with snapping and optimistic updates, concurrency with ETags, accessible grid keyboard model (APG date picker), locale week start / hour cycle / non-Gregorian calendars, calendar component API (controlled value, views, render slots)
topics.takeaway: A calendar is a grid UI on top of a time model. Get the time model right — instants with time zones, floating dates for all-day events, recurrence rules with exceptions — and the UI problems (layout, drag, accessibility) become tractable.

topics.title: Design a Design Tool (Figma-like Canvas)
topics.informs: rendering technology for editors (DOM/SVG vs Canvas 2D vs WebGL vs WebGPU, WASM core), scene-graph document model (normalized nodes, parent pointers, fractional indexing), camera and coordinate transforms, render-on-demand loop with viewport culling and spatial indexes, hit testing and selection, tool state machines and pointer input (coalesced events, pointer capture, pinch), multiplayer sync (server-authoritative LWW vs OT vs CRDT, presence), undo/redo in a shared document, canvas accessibility (parallel DOM, layers tree), plugin sandboxing, export and tainted canvases, persistence and offline
topics.takeaway: A design tool is a document database (a scene graph) + a camera + a GPU renderer + a tool state machine + a sync engine. The DOM is for the panels around the canvas; the canvas itself is your own mini rendering engine.
